faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars that orbit each other. Their orbital plane is tilted so that from Earth, each star periodically passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light. This creates a distinctive dip in the brightness pattern we observe. Eclipsing binaries are valuable laboratories for measuring stellar properties and understanding stellar evolution.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a star system whose light curve shows eclipse-like features but has not yet been checked for false alarms. A 'confirmed' candidate is one that passed Star Vetter's automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the eclipse signature comes from the target star itself and not from a nearby star whose light accidentally blended into the measurement. Confirmation means the automated check passed - it does not mean the star has been scientifically verified by other means.
faqs.question: What do you mean by 'candidate' versus 'confirmed'?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter uses a machine learning model (gradient boosting, trained on 2465 labeled examples) as a second opinion on whether a candidate is likely to be a real eclipsing binary. It scores each candidate but does not decide which ones get checked - every candidate that passes statistical vetting and the catalog cross-match undergoes the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score. The ML score is for reference only and is not used to gate or prioritize future work.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning score shown on candidate pages?

faqs.answer: Every candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This test examines the spatial distribution of the eclipse signal within the TESS pixel data to confirm the eclipse comes from the target star and not from a fainter nearby star whose light contaminated the measurement. The pixel-level check is fully automated and runs on every candidate that passes the earlier statistical and catalog checks.
faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check whether a candidate is real?

faqs.answer: TESS observes stars at a regular cadence, which can create ambiguity: the true eclipse period might be different from what the light curve appears to show. Star Vetter tests for this using an odd/even eclipse-depth test, which compares the brightness dip of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered ones. If they differ significantly, the period may be aliased. This caveat, if present, is listed on the candidate's individual page.
faqs.question: What if the eclipse period looks like it might be aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate on this site has a detailed page with its light curve, vetting statistics, and pixel-level check results. You can download the TESS light curve data and inspect it yourself. Because many of these candidates are still unconfirmed eclipsing binaries in the broader astronomical sense, independent examination and follow-up are encouraged.
faqs.question: Can I verify a candidate myself by looking at the data?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter's pipeline ends once a candidate is listed here. The site does not perform radial-velocity spectroscopy, conduct ground-based follow-up, add candidates to official catalogs, or coordinate with other research teams. Candidates remain listed on this site with their vetting details and caveats for anyone interested in learning more or pursuing further study.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in a plane that crosses our line of sight, so they periodically block each other's light. TESS collects brightness measurements of hundreds of thousands of stars; Star Vetter searches those light curves for the telltale dips that signal an eclipse, then tests whether each candidate is real or a false alarm caused by instrument noise or other stars in the field. Every candidate passes statistical vetting, a cross-check against six known variable-star catalogs, and an automated pixel-level check to rule out contamination from nearby stars. We list the 239 candidates that passed all these gates. You can examine each one's light curve, vetting details, and open caveats on its individual page. Because many candidates remain unconfirmed eclipsing binaries, visitors are encouraged to inspect the data themselves.
